---
title: "Forecasting South African Daily Peak Electricity Demand: Exponential Smoothing vs Time Series Regression"
format: html
---

```{r setup}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(forecast)
library(lubridate)
set.seed(2026)

daily <- readRDS(here::here("data", "eskom_daily_peak.rds"))

```

## Introduction

In Projects 1 and 2 I worked with daily AAPL prices and returns. The models found very little structure in the mean of the returns, and the main problem turned out to be volatility that changes over time. This project moves to a series with a lot of structure in the mean. Electricity demand depends on the day of the week, the time of year and public holidays, which makes it a good series for two of the Section 2 methods, exponential smoothing and time series regression. The two approaches handle this structure in different ways. Exponential smoothing updates a level and a seasonal pattern as each new day comes in, while regression describes demand as a fixed function of time and the calendar.

I use Eskom's daily peak electricity demand from April 2022 to September 2026 and keep the last 365 days as a test year. The data also include Eskom's own day-ahead forecast, which gives a real forecast to compare against, not only simple benchmarks. I compare exponential smoothing models with a time series regression, first fitted by OLS and then with ARMA errors, at one day and seven days ahead.


This project asks three questions.

1. Which approach, exponential smoothing or time series regression, better captures the weekly and yearly cycles in South African daily peak demand?
2. Can either approach match or do better than Eskom's own day-ahead forecast?
3. How reliable are the prediction intervals of each approach, one day and seven days ahead?

I judge the models on the test year, using the RMSE, MAE and MAPE for the point forecasts and the 95% coverage and CRPS for the intervals.


## Define the Series

```{r define series}
nrow(daily)
range(daily$date)
all(diff(daily$date) == 1)
table(daily$n_hours)

summary(daily$peak)

round(prop.table(table(daily$peak_hour)),3)

```

The data comes from the file ESK19847 on the Eskom Data Portal, which gives hourly values. I use the RSA Contracted Demand column, which has 24 hourly values for each day, and take the highest of these as the daily peak. This daily peak is the series I forecast. The same file has Eskom's own hourly forecast of RSA Contracted Demand, and I take its daily maximum in the same way, so Eskom's forecast and my models forecast the same quantity.

The series runs from 1 April 2022 to 27 September 2026, which is 1641 days. There are no gaps between the dates and every day has all 24 hourly values. Hours with a missing demand value are dropped before the hours are counted, so this also shows that no hourly values are missing, and I did not have to fill in or remove any days.

Daily peak demand ranges from 21262 MW to 34666 MW. The median is 28892 MW and the mean is 28802 MW, so the series is not skewed much in either direction. Half of the days sit between 27256 MW and 30410 MW.

The peak almost always happens in the evening. On 62.8% of days it falls in hour 18 and on 35.8% of days in hour 19, which is 98.6% of all days. The other 1.4% of days peak in one of seven hours between hour 6 and hour 17, and none of those hours makes up more than 0.4% of the days. Because nearly every peak comes from the same two hours, the daily maximum measures the same thing from one day to the next.


## Explore

```{r explore time plot}
ggplot(daily, aes(date, peak)) + 
    geom_line(colour = "steelblue") +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Daily Peak Demand (MW)", title = "South African Daily Peak Electricity Demand") +
    theme_minimal()
```

The time plot shows the daily peak over the full data set. Demand rises every winter and falls back in summer, with a sharp drop at the end of each December. The winter peaks also get lower each year, from 34666 MW in 2022 to 30749 MW in 2026, so the overall level of demand is falling.

```{r explore peak hour}
ggplot(daily, aes(factor(peak_hour, levels = 0:23))) +
    geom_bar(fill = "steelblue")+
    scale_x_discrete(drop = FALSE) +
    labs(x = "Hour", y = "Number of days", title = "Hour of the Daily Peak") + 
    theme_minimal()
```

The bar chart shows the hour in which each day's peak occurs. Almost every day peaks in hour 18 or hour 19. The few other days peak in the morning or the afternoon, and each of those hours has fewer than ten days. This confirms the table in Define the Series, so the series I forecast is in practice the evening peak.

```{r explore weekly}
daily <- daily |>
    mutate(dow = wday(date, label = TRUE, week_start = 1),
           month = month(date, label = TRUE),
           year = year(date))

ggplot(daily, aes(dow, peak)) +
    geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.6)+
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Daily peak demand (MW)", title = "Daily Peak Demand by Day of the Week") +
    theme_minimal()

daily |> group_by(dow) |> summarise(mean_peak = round(mean(peak)), .groups = "drop")
```

The boxplot shows the daily peak for each day of the week. Monday to Thursday have similar peaks, with means between 29440 MW and 29593 MW. Friday is lower at 28294 MW, and Saturday, 27568 MW, and Sunday, 27688 MW, are about 1900 MW below the midweek days. The low outliers on the weekdays include the lowest days in the series, which are all public holidays or days in the year-end break, listed at the end of this section. This weekly cycle is why I use a seasonal period of 7 in the exponential smoothing models and weekday indicators in the regression.


```{r explore yearly}
ggplot(daily, aes(month,peak)) +
    geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.6)+
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Daily peak demand (MW)", title = "Daily Peak Demand by Month")  +
    theme_minimal()
daily |> group_by(month) |> summarise(mean_peak = round(mean(peak)), .groups = "drop")
```

The monthly boxplots show the yearly cycle. Demand is highest in June, 30910 MW, and July, 30864 MW, and lowest in December, 26296 MW, and January, 26848 MW. The gap between the highest and lowest month is about 4600 MW, more than twice the gap of about 2000 MW between the highest and lowest day of the week. The low outliers in April are the Easter weekend of 2026, 3 to 5 April, and 25 April 2026, the Saturday of the Freedom Day long weekend. December covers the widest range of values, because it contains both normal working days and the very low days of the year-end break, down to 21335 MW on 25 December 2025.


```{r explore trend}
daily |> 
    filter(month(date) %in% 6:8) |> 
    group_by(year) |>
    summarise(days = n(),
              mean_peak = round(mean(peak)), 
              max_peak = round(max(peak)),
              .groups = "drop") 

```

To see whether demand is changing over the years, I compared the same three winter months, June to August, in each year, so that the yearly cycle does not affect the comparison. The mean winter peak fell every year, from 31679 MW in 2022 to 28394 MW in 2026, and the highest winter peak fell from 34666 MW to 30749 MW. The fall from 2025 to 2026 was 1696 MW, which is much larger than the falls between the earlier years of 450 MW to 680 MW. The winter of 2026 is inside my test year, so the models meet this larger drop out of sample.


```{r explore mstl}
y <- msts(daily$peak, seasonal.periods = c(7, 365.25))

fit_mstl <- mstl(y)
autoplot(fit_mstl) +
  labs(title = "MSTL Decomposition with Periods of 7 and 365.25 Days",
       x = "Year of the Series (1 = 1 April 2022)")
```

To see the two cycles and the trend separately, I decomposed the series with MSTL using periods of 7 and 365.25 days. The trend stays near 30000 MW for about the first ten months, then falls, and falls faster from early 2025 to end near 26200 MW. The yearly component is about 2000 to 3000 MW above the trend in winter and drops to almost 6000 MW below it at the end of each December. The weekly component rises by about 800 to 1300 MW and falls by about 1000 to 2000 MW, and its size changes through the year. The remainder is mostly within 1500 MW of zero, with a few larger spikes that I look at below.

```{r ACF and PACF}
ggtsdisplay(daily$peak, lag.max = 42, main = "Daily Peak Demand with its ACF and PACF", xlab = "Day")
```

The ACF of the daily peak stays high at every lag up to 42 days and dies down slowly, with peaks at lags 7, 14, 21 and so on. The slow decay comes from the slowly moving level and the yearly cycle, and the peaks every seven lags come from the weekly cycle. The PACF has a large spike at lag 1, positive spikes at lags 3 to 7 that are largest at lag 6, and a large negative spike at lag 8, which again points to the weekly cycle. An ACF that decays this slowly is a sign that the series is not stationary, and the models in this project deal with this through the level and seasonal terms in exponential smoothing and the trend and seasonal terms in the regression.

```{r explore remainder}

daily$remainder <- as.numeric(fit_mstl[, "Remainder"])

daily |>
  filter(abs(remainder) > 3 * sd(remainder)) |>
  select(date, dow, peak, remainder) |>
  arrange(date)


daily |>
  arrange(peak) |>
  select(date, dow, peak) |>
  head(10)
```

To find unusual days, I listed the days where the MSTL remainder is more than three standard deviations from zero. There are 15 of these. Nine are too low, and seven of the nine are around Easter. The other two low days are 29 May 2024, which was a public holiday for the national election, and 20 March 2023, the Monday before the Human Rights Day holiday. I cannot explain the six high days from the calendar, and without weather data I cannot check whether they were cold days.

The year-end days are not in this list, even though they are the lowest days in the series. They fall on the same dates every year, so MSTL puts them into the yearly component. Easter moves from year to year, so it ends up in the remainder instead. This is why the regression gets a separate Easter indicator. The year-end break also gets its own indicator, because its drop lasts only a few days and a small number of Fourier terms gives a smooth yearly curve that cannot fall that sharply.

The ten lowest days in the series are all public holidays or days in the year-end break. Eight of them are from the break between 24 December 2025 and 2 January 2026, and the lowest is 1 January 2026 at 21262 MW. Nine of the ten fall inside my test year, so the test year contains the most extreme low days in the data.

## Design the Comparison
```{r train test}
h_test <- 365
n <- nrow(daily)
train <- daily[1:(n - h_test), ]
test <- daily[(n - h_test + 1):n, ]

cat("train:", format(min(train$date)), "to", format(max(train$date)), "-", nrow(train), "days\n")
cat("test: ", format(min(test$date)),  "to", format(max(test$date)),  "-", nrow(test),  "days\n")
```

I held out the last 365 days as a test set, from 28 September 2025 to 27 September 2026, and used the first 1276 days, from 1 April 2022 to 27 September 2025, for training. The test set is a full year, so it contains every season and every public holiday once. All model parameters are estimated on the training data and kept fixed in the test year, and a forecast for a test day only uses data up to the day the forecast is made. I also choose between models using the training data only. The one place the test year comes in before the final comparison is the list of holidays and the Easter days, which I picked by looking at the MSTL remainder of the full series. These are calendar dates that are known in advance, and the same Easter days already stand out in the four training years, so I would have made the same choice without the test year.

```{r benchmark}
source(here::here("projects", "project-03-eskom-demand", "R", "evaluation_functions.R"))

y <- daily$peak
idx <- (n - h_test + 1):n
actual <- y[idx]

bench <- tibble::tibble(
    date = test$date,
    actual = actual,
    naive_1 = y[idx-1],
    snaive_1 = y[idx-7],
    naive_7 = y[idx-7],
    eskom_1 = test$eskom_fc
)

sum(is.na(bench$eskom_1))

res_h1 <- rbind(
    Naive = point_metrics(bench$actual, bench$naive_1),
    Seasonal_Naive = point_metrics(bench$actual, bench$snaive_1),
    Eskom = point_metrics(bench$actual, bench$eskom_1)
)

round(res_h1, 2)
```
 

I compare every model against three benchmarks. The naive forecast uses the peak from the day before. The seasonal naive forecast uses the peak from the same weekday one week earlier. At the seven-day horizon the latest value I have is from a week earlier, so the naive and seasonal naive forecasts are the same thing. The third benchmark is Eskom's own day-ahead forecast, which is available for every day of the test year. It is a one-day-ahead point forecast only, so it is not part of the seven-day comparison or the interval measures.

I measure point accuracy with the RMSE, MAE and MAPE. To judge the prediction intervals I use the coverage of the 95% interval, which is the share of test days whose actual value falls inside it and should be close to 0.95, and the CRPS. The CRPS scores the whole forecast distribution, here a normal distribution with the forecast as its mean, and is lower when the forecast is close to the actual value without being wider than it needs to be. It is in MW, and for a forecast with no spread it reduces to the absolute error, so it can be read on the same scale as the MAE.

The table gives the one-day-ahead scores of the benchmarks on the test year. Eskom's forecast has an RMSE of 622.80 MW, against 959.27 MW for the naive forecast and 1058.72 MW for the seasonal naive forecast. Using yesterday's peak works better than using the same weekday last week. Eskom's forecast is clearly the strongest, with an MAE of 493.57 MW and a MAPE of 1.86%, and this is the standard the models in the next sections are measured against.

```{r check interval}
source(here::here("projects", "project-03-eskom-demand", "R", "evaluation_functions.R"))

crps_norm(actual = 0, mu = 0, sigma = 1)
coverage(actual = 0, lower = -1.96, upper = 1.96)

```

I compute the CRPS with the closed form for a normal forecast distribution. As a check, my function gives 0.23 for an observation at the mean of a standard normal, which matches (√2 − 1)/√π. The coverage function gives 1 for a value of 0 and an interval from −1.96 to 1.96, as it should.

## Simple Exponential Smoothing (Own Code)

```{r ses fit}
source(here::here("projects", "project-03-eskom-demand", "R", "es_functions.R"))

y_train <- train$peak
l0 <- y_train[1]

fit_ses <- nlm(ses_sse, p = 0, y = y_train, l0 = l0)
alpha_hat <- 1/(1 + exp(-fit_ses$estimate))

c(alpha = alpha_hat, SSE = fit_ses$minimum, code = fit_ses$code)

ref <- ses(ts(y_train), initial = "simple", h = 1)
ref$model$par["alpha"]
```

I started with simple exponential smoothing, which I coded by hand. The level starts at the first training value and each day moves by alpha times that day's one-step error, and I estimated alpha by minimising the sum of squared one-step errors with nlm(). To keep alpha between 0 and 1, nlm() works on an unrestricted parameter that is turned into alpha with the logistic function. nlm() stopped with code 1, which means it found a minimum, and the estimated alpha was 1.00 to two decimal places. ses() from the forecast package, started from the same first value, gave the same alpha. An alpha of 1 means each forecast is just the last observed value, so simple exponential smoothing reduces to the naive forecast. The series has a weekly cycle and simple exponential smoothing has no way to include it, so the best it can do is follow yesterday's value. This is why I moved on to models with a seasonal component.

## Holt-Winters and ETS

```{r ets fit}
y7 <- ts(train$peak, frequency = 7)
actual_tr <- train$peak
fits <- list(
    "ETS(A,N,A)"  = ets(y7, model = "ANA"),
    "ETS(A,A,A)"  = ets(y7, model = "AAA", damped = FALSE),
    "ETS(A,Ad,A)" = ets(y7, model = "AAA", damped = TRUE),
    "ETS(M,N,M)"  = ets(y7, model = "MNM"),
    "ETS(M,A,M)"  = ets(y7, model = "MAM", damped = FALSE),
    "ETS(M,Ad,M)" = ets(y7, model = "MAM", damped = TRUE)
    )
getpar <- function(f, nm) unname(f$par[nm])
ets_table <- data.frame(
    model = names(fits),
    AIC = sapply(fits, function(f) f$aicc),
    alpha = sapply(fits, getpar, nm = "alpha"),
    beta  = sapply(fits, getpar, nm = "beta"),
    gamma = sapply(fits, getpar, nm = "gamma"),
    phi   = sapply(fits, getpar, nm = "phi")
)

ets_table <- ets_table[order(ets_table$AIC), ]

train_scores <- function(actual, fc, sigma) {
  c(point_metrics(actual, fc),
    Cover95 = coverage(actual, fc - 1.96 * sigma, fc + 1.96 * sigma),
    CRPS    = crps_norm(actual, fc, sigma))
}

score_fit <- function(f) {
  fc    <- as.numeric(fitted(f))
  sigma <- sqrt(f$sigma2)
  if (f$components[1] == "M") sigma <- sigma * fc   
  train_scores(actual_tr, fc, sigma)
}

train_tab <- t(sapply(fits[ets_table$model], score_fit))   

ets_results <- cbind(ets_table[, -1], train_tab)
round(ets_results, 4)
```


I then fitted six ETS models to the training data with a weekly seasonal period of 7. Three have additive errors and seasonality and three have multiplicative errors and seasonality, and within each group there is a model with no trend, a linear trend and a damped trend. The table gives the AICc and smoothing parameters of each model, together with the scores of its one-step fitted values on the training data.

ETS(A,A,A) has the lowest AICc at 25369.25. ETS(A,N,A) and ETS(A,Ad,A) are only 0.82 and 1.32 higher, and the training RMSEs of the three additive models are within 1.27 MW of each other, so they fit about equally well. ETS(M,Ad,M) has the lowest training RMSE, 564.93 MW against 575.76 MW, and the lowest CRPS, 307.94 against 311.59, but its AICc is 23.13 higher than that of ETS(A,A,A). The AICc is based on the likelihood, and for a model with multiplicative errors the likelihood measures each error relative to the level, not in MW as the RMSE does, so the two can rank models differently. I chose ETS(A,A,A) on the AICc, which adds a penalty for the number of parameters and is the same measure I used to choose the ARIMA models in Project 1. All six models cover between 93.73% and 94.51% of the training values with their 95% intervals, so all are close to 95%.


```{r ets chosen}

fit_ets <- fits[["ETS(A,A,A)"]]
fit_ets            
autoplot(fit_ets)  
```

In ETS(A,A,A) alpha is 0.91, so the level moves most of the way to each new observation. Beta, 0.0017, and gamma, 0.0001, are close to zero, so the slope and the weekly pattern hardly change over the training period. The seven seasonal values range from −1317.13 MW to 835.38 MW, a weekly swing of 2152.51 MW. The three negative values belong to Friday, Saturday and Sunday, with Saturday the lowest, which matches the weekday means in Explore. The standard deviation of the one-step errors is 578.25 MW.

The component plot shows that the level carries the yearly cycle, with highs in winter and a sharp dip at each year-end. The model only has a weekly seasonal term, so the level has to follow the yearly cycle and the holiday drops from one day to the next, which is why alpha is so high. The slope starts at 44.98 MW per day and falls to close to zero by the end of training. The seasonal panel looks like a solid block because the same weekly pattern repeats almost unchanged for 182 weeks.

```{r ets fitted plot}

st  <- fit_ets$states               
win <- (nrow(train) - 41):nrow(train) 

plot_df <- data.frame(
  date     = train$date[win],
  observed = train$peak[win],
  fitted   = as.numeric(fitted(fit_ets))[win],  
  level    = st[win + 1, "l"]                    
)

ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = date)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = observed, colour = "observed")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fitted,   colour = "fitted (one-step forecast)"), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(aes(y = level,    colour = "level")) +
  labs(title = "ETS(A,A,A) fitted values and level, last six weeks of training", x = NULL, y = "daily peak (MW)", colour = NULL)
```

The plot shows the last six weeks of the training data. The level moves less than the observed values, because the weekly pattern is taken out of it, and the fitted values add the weekly pattern back on top of the level, so they rise and fall with the weekdays and the weekends. When demand changes suddenly, the fitted value misses on that day and the level catches up on the next day. This shows at the end of the plot, on Heritage Day (24 September 2025). The fitted value misses the drop, the level falls with demand, and the next day's fitted value is then too low when demand recovers.


```{r ets test 1 day}
y_all <- ts(daily$peak, frequency = 7)

one_step <- function(fit){
    f_all <- ets(y_all, model = fit, use.initial.values = TRUE)
    print(all.equal(as.numeric(fitted(f_all))[1:nrow(train)], as.numeric(fitted(fit))))
    as.numeric(fitted(f_all))[idx]
}

bench$ets_aaa <- one_step(fits[["ETS(A,A,A)"]])

results <- rbind(
    Naive = point_metrics(bench$actual, bench$naive_1),
    SeasonalNaive = point_metrics(bench$actual, bench$snaive_1),
    Eskom = point_metrics(bench$actual, bench$eskom_1),
    ETS_AAA = point_metrics(bench$actual, bench$ets_aaa)
)

round(results,2)

```

To forecast the test year I ran the training model over the full series without re-estimating it. The fitted values on the training part matched the original fit, so the test forecasts only use the training parameters, and each forecast only uses data up to the day before. One day ahead, ETS(A,A,A) has an RMSE of 599.88 MW, an MAE of 442.86 MW and a MAPE of 1.68%, against 622.80 MW, 493.57 MW and 1.86% for Eskom's own forecast. So over the test year ETS(A,A,A) did better than Eskom's forecast on all three measures. Whether this gap is more than chance is a question I come back to in Compare Models.


```{r ets quarter intervals}
sg <- sqrt(fits[["ETS(A,A,A)"]]$sigma2)

bench$lo <- bench$ets_aaa - 1.96 * sg
bench$hi <- bench$ets_aaa + 1.96 * sg
bench$outside <- bench$actual < bench$lo | bench$actual > bench$hi

c(Cover95 = coverage(bench$actual, bench$lo, bench$hi), 
  CRPS = crps_norm(bench$actual, bench$ets_aaa, sg))
bench$panel <- ceiling(seq_len(nrow(bench)) / 92)
bench$panel <- factor(bench$panel, labels = tapply(format(bench$date, "%b %Y"), bench$panel,
                      function(x) paste(x[1], "to", x[length(x)])))

ggplot(bench, aes(x = date)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(aes(y = actual, colour = "actual")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ets_aaa, colour = "ETS(A,A,A) forecast"), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(data = subset(bench, outside), aes(y = actual), colour = "red", size = 1.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol = 1, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(title = "ETS(A,A,A) one-day-ahead forecasts with 95% intervals, test year", x = NULL, y = "daily peak (MW)", colour = NULL,
       caption = "Shaded band: 95% interval. Red points: actuals outside it.") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The plot shows the one-day-ahead forecasts for the test year with their 95% intervals, split into four periods of 92 days. The band has the same width all year, 1133.38 MW either side of the forecast, because the interval is built from the training standard deviation of 578.25 MW. The intervals cover 92.60% of the actual values, so 27 days fall outside them, and the CRPS is 326.65. The intervals are too narrow, as the course notes warn is common (Lecture 2 slides, prediction intervals). Part of the reason is that the test errors, RMSE 599.88 MW, are larger than the training standard deviation. But if the test errors were normal with a standard deviation of 599.88 MW, this band would still cover about 94% of days, so the rest of the shortfall comes from a few very large errors.

The days outside the band are not spread evenly through the year. The biggest group is at the year-end, where demand falls outside the band on both sides. It first drops below the band as the break starts, because the model does not know the holiday is coming. Then in the first days of January it is above the band, because the level has followed demand down and the forecast stays too low while demand recovers. The same pattern shows up in late April around Freedom Day on 27 April, and Heritage Day at the end of the test year also falls outside.

The other red points are mostly single days spread through the year, such as 11 August 2026, when the peak jumped to 30614 MW. This is one of the high days that stood out in the MSTL remainder in Explore, and without weather data I cannot say what caused it. In February, March, May and June almost every day is inside the band, so the intervals work well in normal weeks and fail mainly around holidays.


```{r ets test 7 day}
horizon <- 7
origins <- (n - h_test + 1 - horizon):(n - horizon)

fc7 <- t(sapply(origins, function(x) {
    f <- ets(ts(y[1:x], frequency = 7), model = fits[["ETS(A,A,A)"]], use.initial.values = TRUE)
    fc <- forecast(f, h = horizon, level = 95)
    c(mean = fc$mean[horizon], lo = fc$lower[horizon], hi = fc$upper[horizon])
}))

bench$ets7 <- fc7[, "mean"]
bench$ets7_lo <- fc7[, "lo"]
bench$ets7_hi <- fc7[, "hi"]

sd7 <- (bench$ets7_hi - bench$ets7_lo) / (2 * 1.96)

res_h7 <- rbind(
    Naive_7 = c(point_metrics(bench$actual, bench$naive_7), Cover95 = NA, CRPS = NA),
    ETS_AAA = c(point_metrics(bench$actual, bench$ets7), 
                Cover95 = coverage(bench$actual, bench$ets7_lo, bench$ets7_hi), 
                CRPS = crps_norm(bench$actual, bench$ets7, sd7))
)

round(res_h7, 3)

```

At the seven-day horizon ETS(A,A,A) has an RMSE of 1056.04 MW and an MAE of 802.37 MW, almost the same as the seasonal naive forecast at 1058.72 MW and 804.01 MW. With alpha close to 1 the level is almost the latest value with its weekly effect taken out, and seven days ahead the model adds back the effect of the same weekday, so its forecast is close to the value on that weekday a week earlier, which is the seasonal naive forecast. The 95% intervals cover 98.4% of the actual values, so they are too wide. For ETS(A,N,N) the h-step forecast variance is σ²[1 + α²(h − 1)] (course notes, Chapter 1, Exercise 10.1), and with beta and gamma close to zero ETS(A,A,A) behaves almost the same way. With alpha at 0.91, each extra day adds about 0.82σ² to the variance. The standard deviation behind the seven-day intervals is 1428.10 MW on average, against an actual RMSE of 1056.04 MW, so the intervals are built for larger errors than the model makes.

```{r ets vs eskom plot}

bench$panel <- ceiling(seq_len(nrow(bench)) / 92)
bench$panel <- factor(bench$panel, labels = tapply(format(bench$date, "%b %Y"), bench$panel, function(x) paste(x[1], "to", x[length(x)])))

ggplot(bench, aes(x = date)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = actual, colour = "actual"), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ets_aaa, colour = "ETS(A,A,A) forecast"), linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_line(aes(y = eskom_1, colour = "Eskom forecast"), linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("actual" = "blue",
                                 "ETS(A,A,A) forecast" = "green",
                                 "Eskom forecast" = "red")) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol = 1, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(title = "One-day-ahead forecasts on the test year: ETS(A,A,A) vs Eskom",
       x = NULL, y = "daily peak (MW)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Through most of the year the ETS and Eskom forecasts are close to each other and to the actual demand. The biggest misses for ETS are around holidays. ETS does not know a holiday is coming, so it misses the drop on the day and then forecasts too low on the next day, because the level has fallen with the holiday. This shows clearly at the year-end, where the ETS forecast drops to about 20000 MW while the actual demand never goes below 21262 MW. Eskom's forecast drops on some holidays themselves, for example on 16 December, where the ETS forecast is still high, so it seems to use the calendar. It has misses of its own, such as in mid-August, when it went above 31000 MW against an actual peak of 30749 MW.


## Exponential Smoothing Diagnostics

```{r ets diagnostic}

checkresiduals(fit_ets, lag = 28)

```

The residuals of ETS(A,A,A) on the training data are centred on zero with no trend, and their spread looks about the same throughout. The largest errors are single days and are more often positive than negative, going up to about 3000 MW against about −2500 MW at the low end. A positive residual means demand was higher than forecast, which fits the days after a holiday, when the level has dropped and the forecast is too low.

The ACF has spikes outside the bands at lags 7, 14, 21 and 28, between about 0.10 and 0.13, and negative spikes at lags 2 to 4 of about −0.12 to −0.15. The value at lag 1 is close to zero, so from one day to the next the level adjusts quickly enough. The Ljung-Box test over 28 lags gives Q* = 190.13 with p < 2.2e-16, so the residuals are not white noise.

The spikes at multiples of 7 mean part of the weekly pattern is left over. The weekly pattern in the model is fixed, with gamma equal to 0.0001, but in the MSTL in Explore the size of the weekly swing changed through the year, so in some weeks the fixed pattern is too big and in others too small. The negative values at lags 2 to 4 mean that an error in one direction tends to be followed a few days later by errors in the other direction. One possible reason is the holiday problem from the test plots, where a one-off drop is mostly passed into the level and the forecasts for the next few days are then off in the other direction.

The histogram is centred on zero but is taller and narrower in the middle than the normal curve, with longer tails out to about −2500 MW and 3000 MW. Most days have small errors and a few days have very large ones. The prediction intervals assume normal errors, so this is the most likely reason the one-day intervals cover fewer test days than the larger test RMSE alone would explain.

ETS(A,A,A) gives one-day forecasts that do better than Eskom's on the test year, but its residuals still contain the holidays and part of the weekly pattern. The regression in the next section adds holiday indicators and a yearly seasonal term directly, which targets the holiday problem. It still uses a fixed weekly pattern through the weekday indicators, so the left-over weekly structure may remain.

## Time Series Regression (OLS)

```{r holidays}

hol <- tibble::tibble(
  date = as.Date(c(
    # 2022
    "2022-04-15","2022-04-18","2022-04-27","2022-05-02","2022-06-16","2022-08-09",
    "2022-12-16","2022-12-26","2022-12-27",
    # 2023
    "2023-01-02","2023-03-21","2023-04-07","2023-04-10","2023-04-27","2023-05-01",
    "2023-06-16","2023-08-09","2023-09-25","2023-12-15","2023-12-25","2023-12-26",
    # 2024
    "2024-01-01","2024-03-21","2024-03-29","2024-04-01","2024-05-01","2024-05-29",
    "2024-06-17","2024-08-09","2024-09-24","2024-12-16","2024-12-25","2024-12-26",
    # 2025
    "2025-01-01","2025-03-21","2025-04-18","2025-04-21","2025-04-28","2025-05-01",
    "2025-06-16","2025-09-24","2025-12-16","2025-12-25","2025-12-26",
    # 2026
    "2026-01-01","2026-04-03","2026-04-06","2026-04-27","2026-05-01","2026-06-16",
    "2026-08-10","2026-09-24"))
)

# checks: all weekdays and all inside the data range
table(wday(hol$date, week_start = 1))
all(hol$date >= min(daily$date) & hol$date <= max(daily$date))

daily$holiday <- daily$date %in% hol$date

# do holidays really show up as low demand?
daily |> filter(holiday) |> summarise(n = n(), mean_remainder = mean(remainder))

# big negative remainders NOT on the list = possible missing holidays or bridge days
daily |> filter(!holiday, remainder < -2 * sd(remainder)) |>
  select(date, peak, remainder) |> arrange(remainder)

daily |>
  filter(!holiday, remainder < -2 * sd(remainder)) |>
  mutate(weekday = wday(date, label = TRUE, week_start = 1)) |>
  select(date, weekday, peak, remainder) |>
  arrange(date) |>
  print(n = 28)
```

Explore showed that the lowest days are holidays, so before fitting the regression I built a list of South African public holidays in the data period. Dummy variables are the usual way to include public holidays in a time series regression (course notes, Chapter 2, Section 3). I only kept holidays that fall on a weekday, because a holiday on a Saturday or Sunday is already a low day and the weekday terms cover it. This gives 52 holidays, including the substitute Mondays and the special holidays on 15 December 2023 and on 29 May 2024, the day of the national election. On these 52 days the MSTL remainder from Explore has a mean of −575 MW, so holidays are clearly lower than the weekly and yearly patterns expect.

To check for low days that the list misses, I looked at the non-holiday days with an MSTL remainder below minus two standard deviations. There are 28 of these. Eleven are the days around Easter that are not public holidays, the Thursday before Good Friday and the Saturday and Sunday of the Easter weekend. Two are bridge days, Mondays before a Tuesday public holiday, and two are weekend days of long weekends, 7 August 2022 and 25 April 2026. Another eleven are in May 2024, and the last two, 30 July and 12 August 2022, I cannot link to the calendar.

```{r regressors}
easter_sun  <- as.Date(c("2022-04-17", "2023-04-09", "2024-03-31", "2025-04-20", "2026-04-05"))
easter_days <- c(easter_sun - 3, easter_sun - 1, easter_sun)

md <- format(daily$date, "%m-%d")

daily$holiday <- daily$date %in% hol$date
daily$easter  <- daily$date %in% easter_days
daily$yearend <- md >= "12-24" | md <= "01-02"


colSums(daily[, c("holiday", "easter", "yearend")])


train <- daily[1:(n - h_test), ]
test  <- daily[(n - h_test + 1):n, ]
```

Based on this I added two more indicators. The Easter indicator covers the Thursday, Saturday and Sunday of each Easter weekend, which is 15 days. The year-end indicator covers 24 December to 2 January, the festive period from Christmas Eve to the day after New Year's Day, which is 40 days over the four year-end breaks. I did not add bridge days or anything for May 2024, so those days stay in the errors.

```{r regression k}
t0 <- min(daily$date)

reg_data <- function(df,K){
    tt  <- as.numeric(df$date - t0) + 1
  out <- data.frame(peak = df$peak, t = tt,
                    dow  = factor(wday(df$date, week_start = 1), levels = 1:7,
                                  labels = c("Mon","Tue","Wed","Thu","Fri","Sat","Sun")))
  for (k in 1:K) {
    out[[paste0("S", k)]] <- sin(2 * pi * k * tt / 365.25)
    out[[paste0("C", k)]] <- cos(2 * pi * k * tt / 365.25)
  }
  out
}

aicc <- function(fit){
    k <- length(coef(fit)) + 1
    n <- nobs(fit)
    AIC(fit) + 2 * k * (k + 1) / (n - k - 1)
}

K_tab <- sapply(1:10, function(K) {
  fit <- lm(peak ~ ., data = reg_data(train, K))
  c(K = K, AICc = aicc(fit), RMSE = sqrt(mean(residuals(fit)^2)))
})
round(t(K_tab), 1)

```

```{r regression K full}

reg_data <- function(df, K, extras = TRUE) {
  tt  <- as.numeric(df$date - t0) + 1
  out <- data.frame(peak = df$peak, t = tt,
                    dow  = factor(wday(df$date, week_start = 1), levels = 1:7,
                                  labels = c("Mon","Tue","Wed","Thu","Fri","Sat","Sun")))
  if (extras) {
    out$holiday <- as.numeric(df$holiday)
    out$easter  <- as.numeric(df$easter)
    out$yearend <- as.numeric(df$yearend)
  }
  for (k in 1:K) {
    out[[paste0("S", k)]] <- sin(2 * pi * k * tt / 365.25)
    out[[paste0("C", k)]] <- cos(2 * pi * k * tt / 365.25)
  }
  out
}

K_full <- sapply(1:10, function(K) {
  fit <- lm(peak ~ ., data = reg_data(train, K, extras = TRUE))
  c(K = K, AICc = aicc(fit), RMSE = sqrt(mean(residuals(fit)^2)))
})
round(t(K_full), 1)
```

The regression has a linear trend, weekday indicators and K pairs of sine and cosine terms with a period of 365.25 days for the yearly cycle (course notes, Chapter 2, Section 3). I chose K by AICc on the training data, trying K from 1 to 10. Without the holiday indicators the AICc falls from 21298.9 at K = 1 to 20520.5 at K = 9 and then goes up by 1.3 at K = 10. With the holiday, Easter and year-end indicators the minimum is also at K = 9, with an AICc of 20222.2, and K = 10 is 1.6 higher. So I used K = 9. It takes this many terms because the yearly pattern is not a simple wave, with a winter hump and a sharp dip at the year-end.

```{r regression fit}

K_opt <- 9

d_full <- reg_data(train, K_opt, extras = TRUE)

fit_reg0 <- lm(peak ~ ., data = reg_data(train, K_opt, extras = FALSE))                      
fit_reg1 <- lm(peak ~ ., data = d_full[, !names(d_full) %in% c("easter", "yearend")])   
fit_reg2 <- lm(peak ~ ., data = d_full)                                                      

rmse_tr <- sapply(list(base = fit_reg0, holiday = fit_reg1, full = fit_reg2),
                  function(f) sqrt(mean(residuals(f)^2)))
round(rmse_tr, 1)

cf <- coef(summary(fit_reg2))
round(cf[!grepl("^(S|C)[0-9]", rownames(cf)), ], 2)
```

I fitted the regression in three stages to see how much each group of indicators adds. The training RMSE is 735.4 MW for the base model with trend, weekday and Fourier terms. Adding the holiday indicator brings it down to 681.3 MW, and adding the Easter and year-end indicators brings it down to 652.6 MW. The training RMSE always falls when terms are added, so the AICc is the fairer check. At K = 9 it falls from 20520.5 without the indicators to 20222.2 with all three, so I kept the full model.

The trend is −1.72 MW per day, which is about 628 MW lower each year. Compared with Monday, Tuesday to Thursday are not significantly different, while Friday is 1286.77 MW lower, Saturday 2094.08 MW lower and Sunday 1973.51 MW lower. A weekday public holiday lowers the peak by 1537.92 MW, an Easter day by 1469.77 MW and a year-end day by 1293.01 MW. On a weekday Christmas Day, Day of Goodwill or New Year's Day both the holiday and the year-end indicators apply, so the model lowers the peak by 2830.93 MW. These standard errors come from OLS, which assumes the errors are independent. When the errors are autocorrelated, OLS standard errors can be very wrong (course notes, Chapter 2, Section 4), so I check this in the diagnostics below.

```{r reg test socres}

d_test <- reg_data(test, K_opt, extras = TRUE)

newdata_list <- list(
  base    = reg_data(test, K_opt, extras = FALSE),
  holiday = d_test[, !names(d_test) %in% c("easter", "yearend")],
  full    = d_test
)
fits_reg <- list(base = fit_reg0, holiday = fit_reg1, full = fit_reg2)

score_reg <- function(fit, newd) {
  p  <- predict(fit, newdata = newd, interval = "prediction", level = 0.95)
  sd <- (p[, "upr"] - p[, "lwr"]) / (2 * qt(0.975, fit$df.residual))
  c(point_metrics(bench$actual, p[, "fit"]),
    Cover95 = coverage(bench$actual, p[, "lwr"], p[, "upr"]),
    CRPS    = crps_norm(bench$actual, p[, "fit"], sd))
}

res_reg <- t(sapply(names(fits_reg), function(nm) score_reg(fits_reg[[nm]], newdata_list[[nm]])))
round(res_reg, 3)
```

On the test year the full regression has an RMSE of 1310.56 MW, an MAE of 1178.01 MW and a MAPE of 4.47%. The base and holiday-only models are about the same, with RMSEs of 1351.80 MW and 1329.54 MW. All three are worse than the naive forecast, 959.27 MW, and much worse than ETS(A,A,A), 599.88 MW, and Eskom, 622.80 MW. The intervals are also poor. Coverage falls from 71.0% to 64.1% to 60.0% as indicators are added, because each stage fits the training data more tightly and gives narrower intervals, while the forecasts themselves stay in the wrong place. The CRPS gets slightly worse at each stage too, from 855.29 to 870.46.

```{r reg bias}
p_full <- predict(fit_reg2, newdata = newdata_list$full)
err <- bench$actual - p_full
mean(err)
block <- ceiling(seq_len(nrow(bench)) / 92)
data.frame(block = 1:4, from = tapply(format(bench$date), block, function(x) x[1]), to = tapply(format(bench$date), block, function(x) x[length(x)]), mean_error = round(tapply(err, block, mean), 0))


```

The forecasts are too high on average by 1122.71 MW across the test year, which is almost the whole MAE of 1178.01 MW. The mean error is about the same in each quarter of the test year, −1178, −1139, −1207 and −962 MW, so the problem is a shift in level, not a slope that gets worse over time. The bias makes up most of the RMSE. With a mean error of 1122.71 MW and an RMSE of 1310.56 MW, the errors around the bias have a standard deviation of only about 676 MW, and the bias accounts for 73% of the mean squared error.


```{r reg train resid}
res_tr <- residuals(fit_reg2)
blk <- ceiling(seq_along(res_tr)/319)

data.frame(block = 1:4, from = tapply(format(train$date), blk, function(x) x[1]), to = tapply(format(train$date), blk, function(x) x[length(x)]), mean_resid = round(tapply(res_tr, blk, mean), 0))

```

To see whether the bias was already there in the training data, I split the training residuals into four blocks of 319 days. The mean residual in each block is small, between −131 MW and 229 MW, so on average the model fitted the training period well. The residual plot in the diagnostics below shows the drop starting in the last few weeks of training, but that is too short to move the block average much.

The linear trend is the most likely cause of the bias in the test year. The model lowers demand by about 628 MW a year, which is close to the falls between the winters of 2022 to 2025 in Explore, 450 MW to 680 MW. Between the 2025 and 2026 winters demand fell by 1696 MW, and a fixed linear trend has no way of following that.

```{r reg forecast plot}
bench$reg_full <- as.numeric(predict(fit_reg2, newdata = newdata_list$full))
bench$panel <- ceiling(seq_len(nrow(bench)) / 92)
bench$panel <- factor(bench$panel, labels = tapply(format(bench$date, "%b %Y"), bench$panel, function(x) paste(x[1], "to", x[length(x)])))

ggplot(bench, aes(x = date)) +
    geom_line(aes(y = actual, colour = "actual"), linewidth = 0.9) +
    geom_line(aes(y = reg_full, colour = "regression forecast"), linewidth = 0.6) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("actual" = "blue", "regression forecast" = "firebrick")) +
    facet_wrap( ~ panel, ncol = 1, scales = "free_x") +
    labs(title = "Regression forecast vs actual on the test year", x = NULL, y = "daily peak (MW)", colour = NULL) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")

```

The plot shows the regression forecasts against the actual demand in the test year. The forecast has the right shape, with the weekly up and down and the big drop at the year-end, where the two lines meet. But it sits above the actual demand almost all year, mostly by 1000 to 2000 MW, and the gap is smallest in June. Demand is clearly above the forecast on only a few days, such as in mid-August and early September.

The weekday, holiday and Fourier terms only move the forecast up and down around a level, and that level comes from the intercept and the linear trend, both fixed on the training data. Nothing in the model uses the most recent demand, so it has no way of seeing that the level has dropped. So the regression gets the calendar right and the level wrong.

```{r reg residuals}
checkresiduals(fit_reg2, lag = 28)
```

The residuals on the training data stay above or below zero for weeks at a time instead of jumping around it. By the last few weeks of the training period they are already 1000 to 1600 MW below zero, which is the start of the level shift that the test year shows. The ACF is 0.65 at lag 1 and dies down slowly, with small bumps at multiples of 7. The Breusch-Godfrey test over 28 lags gives LM = 613.6 with p < 2.2e-16, so the errors are strongly autocorrelated. The histogram is close to normal with a few large positive errors.

This means the OLS standard errors in the coefficient table cannot be trusted, and that each day's error carries information about the next day's error. The regression with ARMA errors in the next section uses this.

## Regression with ARMA Errors

```{r reg PACF}
ggtsdisplay(residuals(fit_reg2), lag.max = 28)
```

To choose a model for the errors I looked at the ACF and PACF of the OLS residuals. The PACF has one large spike of about 0.65 at lag 1 and only small values after it, apart from a spike of about 0.12 at lag 6. The ACF dies down gradually, at about 0.65, 0.45, 0.31 and 0.23 for the first four lags. That is close to the powers of 0.65 (0.65, 0.42, 0.27, 0.18) that an AR(1) would give, decaying just a little more slowly. A PACF that cuts off after lag 1 with an ACF that tails off is the pattern of an AR(1) in the identification table of the course notes (Part 1, Section 6.4, Table 22). The ACF also has small bumps at lags 7, 14, 21 and 28 from weekly structure. Together this points to an AR(1) for the errors.

```{r reg ARMA models}

make_xreg <- function(x) {
  X <- model.matrix(peak ~ ., data = x)[, -1]
  X[, "t"] <- X[, "t"] / 1000
  X
}

d_train <- reg_data(train, K_opt)
d_test  <- reg_data(test,  K_opt)

xreg_train <- make_xreg(d_train)
xreg_test  <- make_xreg(d_test)

orders <- list("AR(1)" = c(1,0,0), "AR(2)" = c(2,0,0), "AR(3)" = c(3,0,0),
               "ARMA(1,1)" = c(1,0,1), "ARMA(2,1)" = c(2,0,1))

fits_arma <- lapply(orders, function(x)
  arima(d_train$peak, order = x, xreg = xreg_train,
        include.mean = TRUE, method = "ML"))

arma_table <- data.frame(
  Model = names(fits_arma),
  AICc  = sapply(fits_arma, function(x) {
    k <- length(coef(x)) + 1; n <- x$nobs
    AIC(x) + 2*k*(k+1)/(n-k-1)
  }),
  RMSE_train = sapply(fits_arma, function(x) sqrt(x$sigma2))
)

arma_table[order(arma_table$AICc), ]

```

I fitted the full regression with five different error models using arima(), with the same regressors as the OLS model, and compared them by AICc on the training data. AR(1) has the lowest AICc at 19432.64. The other four are between 1.15 and 3.17 higher, and all five have a one-step error standard deviation between 478.21 MW and 478.45 MW. The extra AR and MA terms add almost nothing, so I kept AR(1), the simplest. Compared with the OLS regression the AICc falls from 20222.2 to 19432.64, which shows how much the model gains from allowing for the autocorrelation.

```{r reg arma chosen}
fit_arma <- fits_arma[["AR(1)"]]
fit_arma$coef[c("ar1", "intercept")]

ggtsdisplay(residuals(fit_arma), lag.max = 28)
```

In the chosen model the AR coefficient is 0.70, so about 70% of each day's gap between demand and the regression line carries over to the next day. One day ahead the forecast therefore adds back about 70% of yesterday's gap. After seven days only 0.70⁷, or about 8%, of it is left.

The residuals of the AR(1) model no longer stay above or below zero for weeks at a time, and the value at lag 1 is close to zero. Most of the ACF and PACF values are now inside the bands. What is left are spikes of about 0.11 to 0.14 at lags 7, 14, 21 and 28. This is weekly structure that the fixed weekday terms do not capture, the same thing that was left in the ETS residuals.

```{r reg arma test 1 day}
y_all <- c(d_train$peak, d_test$peak)
xreg_all <- rbind(xreg_train, xreg_test)

fit_all <- arima(y_all, order = c(1,0,0), xreg = xreg_all, include.mean = TRUE, fixed = coef(fit_arma), transform.pars = FALSE, method = "ML")

all.equal(as.numeric(residuals(fit_all))[1:nrow(train)], as.numeric(residuals(fit_arma)), tolerance = 1e-4)

fc_all <- y_all - as.numeric(residuals(fit_all))
bench$arma1 <- fc_all[idx]

sg <- sqrt(fit_arma$sigma2)
bench$arma1_lo <- bench$arma1 - 1.96 *sg
bench$arma1_hi <- bench$arma1 + 1.96 * sg

res_arma <- c(point_metrics(actual,bench$arma1), Cover95 = coverage(actual, bench$arma1_lo, bench$arma1_hi), CRPS = crps_norm(actual , bench$arma1, sg))

round(res_arma, 3)

```

To forecast the test year I ran the AR(1) model over the full series with the parameters fixed at the training estimates. The residuals on the training part matched the original fit, so the test forecasts only use the training parameters, and each forecast only uses data up to the day before. One day ahead, the RMSE is 606.36 MW, the MAE 493.03 MW and the MAPE 1.87%. This is a large improvement on the OLS regression, RMSE 1310.56 MW. It has a slightly lower RMSE than Eskom, 622.80 MW, and almost the same MAE, 493.03 against 493.57 MW, but it is behind ETS(A,A,A), which has an RMSE of 599.88 MW and an MAE of 442.86 MW.

The 95% intervals cover 87.1% of the test days and the CRPS is 348.91. The intervals are too narrow because they are built from the training error standard deviation of 478.45 MW, while the test RMSE is 606.36 MW. If the test errors were normal with that standard deviation, a band of 937.76 MW either side would cover about 88% of days, close to the 87.1% here. So for this model the larger test errors explain almost all of the shortfall, unlike ETS(A,A,A), where heavy tails also played a part.

```{r reg arma 1 forecast}
bench$panel <- ceiling(seq_len(nrow(bench)) / 92)
bench$panel <- factor(bench$panel, labels = tapply(format(bench$date, "%b %Y"), bench$panel,
                      function(x) paste(x[1], "to", x[length(x)])))

ggplot(bench, aes(x = date)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = actual, colour = "actual"), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_line(aes(y = arma1, colour = "Regression + AR(1) forecast"), linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_line(aes(y = eskom_1, colour = "Eskom forecast"), linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("actual" = "blue",
                                 "Regression + AR(1) forecast" = "darkorange",
                                 "Eskom forecast" = "red")) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol = 1, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(title = "One-day-ahead forecasts on the test year: Regression + AR(1) vs Eskom",
       x = NULL, y = "daily peak (MW)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The plot shows the one-day forecasts of the regression with AR(1) errors against the actual demand and Eskom's forecast. The constant gap of the OLS forecast is gone, and the forecast now follows the actual demand closely through the whole year, with the weekly pattern and the year-end drop in the right place. For most of the year it is hard to tell apart from Eskom's forecast.

The AR(1) term is what closes the gap. Each day the forecast adds back about 70% of the previous day's gap between demand and the regression line, so when demand runs below the regression level, the next forecast is pulled down towards it. It does not close the whole gap, because 30% of the gap is not carried over. With a level error of 1122.71 MW in the OLS model, that should leave the forecast about 339 MW too high on average, and the mean error on the test year is −339.88 MW, which matches. This is why the forecast still sits slightly above the actual demand on many days, especially in June and September.

The model still misses after sudden changes. In the Easter dip in early April and the drop around Freedom Day in late April, the forecast does not go as low as the actual demand and then stays low for a day after demand has recovered. The holiday and Easter indicators lower the forecast on those days, but only by their average effect in the training years, and the AR(1) term then carries the miss into the next day. In mid-August, when the peak jumped to 30749 MW, the forecast only reached about 30200 MW and was a day late. That jump has no calendar reason, and the AR(1) term only learns from yesterday's gap, so it can follow a change in level but cannot see a one-off day coming.

```{r reg arma test 7 day}

horizon <- 7
phi     <- as.numeric(coef(fit_arma)["ar1"])

fc7 <- numeric(length(idx))
for (i in seq_along(idx)) {
  o  <- idx[i] - horizon                      # forecast origin
  fo <- arima(y_all[1:o], order = c(1, 0, 0), xreg = xreg_all[1:o, ],
              include.mean = TRUE, fixed = coef(fit_arma),
              transform.pars = FALSE, method = "ML")
  pr <- predict(fo, n.ahead = horizon,
                newxreg = xreg_all[(o + 1):(o + horizon), , drop = FALSE])
  fc7[i] <- pr$pred[horizon]
}
bench$arma7 <- fc7

# AR(1) forecast-error sd at horizon h: sigma * sqrt(1 + phi^2 + ... + phi^(2(h-1)))
sd7 <- sg * sqrt(sum(phi^(2 * (0:(horizon - 1)))))
bench$arma7_lo <- bench$arma7 - 1.96 * sd7
bench$arma7_hi <- bench$arma7 + 1.96 * sd7

res_arma7 <- c(point_metrics(actual, bench$arma7),
               Cover95 = coverage(actual, bench$arma7_lo, bench$arma7_hi),
               CRPS    = crps_norm(actual, bench$arma7, sd7))
round(res_arma7, 3)

```

At seven days ahead the regression with AR(1) errors has an RMSE of 1236.37 MW, an MAE of 1093.65 MW and a MAPE of 4.16%. This is only a little better than the OLS regression, 1310.56 MW, and worse than both ETS(A,A,A), 1056.04 MW, and the seasonal naive forecast, 1058.72 MW. With only about 8% of the latest gap left after seven steps, the forecast falls back almost all the way to the OLS level, which is too high. The 95% intervals, 1305.37 MW either side of the forecast, cover only 66.6% of the test days because the forecasts themselves are in the wrong place.

The AR(1) errors fix the level problem one day ahead, where the model now matches Eskom, but not seven days ahead, where the forecast drifts back to the OLS level. At the longer horizon the regression still has the calendar right and the level wrong.


## Compare Models

```{r model comparison}
score_row <- function(actual, fc, lo = NULL, hi = NULL) {
  out <- point_metrics(actual, fc)
  if (is.null(lo)) return(c(out, Cover95 = NA, CRPS = NA))
  sgm <- (hi - lo) / (2 * 1.96)
  c(out, Cover95 = coverage(actual, lo, hi), CRPS = crps_norm(actual, fc, sgm))
}

# plain regression: forecast and prediction interval from the OLS fit
pr_ols <- predict(fit_reg2, newdata = d_test, interval = "prediction")
bench$reg_full <- pr_ols[, "fit"]
bench$reg_lo   <- pr_ols[, "lwr"]
bench$reg_hi   <- pr_ols[, "upr"]

res1 <- rbind(
  "Naive"              = score_row(actual, bench$naive_1),
  "Seasonal naive"     = score_row(actual, bench$snaive_1),
  "Eskom"              = score_row(actual, bench$eskom_1),
  "ETS(A,A,A)"         = score_row(actual, bench$ets_aaa, bench$lo, bench$hi),
  "Regression"         = score_row(actual, bench$reg_full, bench$reg_lo, bench$reg_hi),
  "Regression + AR(1)" = score_row(actual, bench$arma1, bench$arma1_lo, bench$arma1_hi))

res7 <- rbind(
  "Seasonal naive"     = score_row(actual, bench$naive_7),
  "ETS(A,A,A)"         = score_row(actual, bench$ets7, bench$ets7_lo, bench$ets7_hi),
  "Regression"         = score_row(actual, bench$reg_full, bench$reg_lo, bench$reg_hi),
  "Regression + AR(1)" = score_row(actual, bench$arma7, bench$arma7_lo, bench$arma7_hi))

round(res1, 3)
round(res7, 3)
```

To compare the models I put all the test-year scores into one table for each horizon. The interval scores use each model's own 95% interval, with the standard deviation taken from the width of the interval. The plain regression only uses calendar regressors that are known in advance, so its forecast and its scores are the same at both horizons. Eskom and the naive forecast only appear in the one-day table, because Eskom only gives a one-day forecast and the seven-day naive forecast is the same as the seasonal naive one.

One day ahead, ETS(A,A,A) has the lowest error on every measure, with an RMSE of 599.88 MW, an MAE of 442.86 MW and a MAPE of 1.68%. The regression with AR(1) errors is next with an RMSE of 606.36 MW, and it is level with Eskom on MAE, 493.03 against 493.57 MW. Both models have a lower RMSE than Eskom, by 22.92 MW and 16.44 MW. These differences are small, 3.68% and 2.64% of Eskom's RMSE, and I have not tested whether they are statistically significant. The gap to the benchmarks is much larger. ETS(A,A,A), the regression with AR(1) errors and Eskom all have an RMSE between 35.08% and 37.47% lower than the naive forecast, 959.27 MW, while the plain regression is the worst model at 1310.56 MW.

ETS(A,A,A) also has the better intervals at one day. Its 95% intervals cover 92.60% of the test days against 87.1% for the regression with AR(1) errors, and its CRPS is lower, 326.65 against 348.91. Both sets of intervals are a little too narrow. The plain regression's intervals cover only 60.0% of the days, because its forecasts are in the wrong place.

Seven days ahead the picture changes. ETS(A,A,A) and the seasonal naive forecast are almost the same, with RMSEs of 1056.04 MW and 1058.72 MW, only 2.68 MW apart. The regression with AR(1) errors falls back to 1236.37 MW, close to the plain regression at 1310.56 MW. At this horizon no model beats the seasonal naive forecast by a meaningful amount. For the intervals, ETS(A,A,A) covers 98.4% of the days, so its intervals are too wide, while the regression with AR(1) errors covers only 66.6%, because its intervals are centred too high. ETS(A,A,A) still has the lower CRPS, 602.15 against 799.94.


```{r model comaprison graph}
comp <- rbind(
  data.frame(Horizon = "1 day",  Model = rownames(res1), RMSE = res1[, "RMSE"], row.names = NULL),
  data.frame(Horizon = "7 days", Model = rownames(res7), RMSE = res7[, "RMSE"], row.names = NULL))
comp$Model <- factor(comp$Model, levels = c("Naive", "Seasonal naive", "Eskom",
                     "ETS(A,A,A)", "Regression", "Regression + AR(1)"))

ggplot(comp, aes(x = Model, y = RMSE)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(RMSE)), vjust = -0.4, size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~ Horizon) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "RMSE (MW)", title = "Test-year RMSE by model and horizon") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
```


The bar chart shows the same RMSEs side by side. At one day, ETS(A,A,A), the regression with AR(1) errors and Eskom sit together at around 600 MW, well below the naive benchmarks and the plain regression. At seven days every model is between 1056.04 MW and 1310.56 MW, and the gap between the best model and the seasonal naive forecast has gone. Naive and Eskom have no bars in the seven-day panel because they are not part of that comparison.

## Forecast and Report

```{r froecast plot setup}

dir.create(here::here("projects", "project-03-eskom-demand", "figures"), showWarnings = FALSE)

bench$panel <- ceiling(seq_len(nrow(bench)) / 92)
bench$panel <- factor(bench$panel, labels = tapply(format(bench$date, "%b %Y"), bench$panel,
                      function(x) paste(x[1], "to", x[length(x)])))

plot_fc <- function(fc, lo, hi, title, file) {
  df <- data.frame(date = bench$date, panel = bench$panel,
                   actual = actual, fc = fc, lo = lo, hi = hi)
  p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = date)) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.25) +
    geom_line(aes(y = actual, colour = "actual"), linewidth = 0.8) +
    geom_line(aes(y = fc, colour = "forecast"), linewidth = 0.6) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("actual" = "grey30", "forecast" = "firebrick")) +
    facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol = 1, scales = "free_x") +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Daily Peak Demand (MW)", colour = NULL,
         title = title, subtitle = "Shaded band: 95% prediction interval") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
  ggsave(here::here("projects", "project-03-eskom-demand", "figures", file),
         p, width = 8, height = 10, bg = "white")
  p
}
```

This section shows the test-year forecasts of the two main models, ETS(A,A,A) and the regression with AR(1) errors, with their 95% prediction intervals at one day and seven days ahead. The scores in the previous section say how well each model did overall. These plots show where in the year the forecasts and intervals work and where they fail.

```{r fc ets h1}
#| label: fc-ets-h1
print(plot_fc(bench$ets_aaa, bench$lo, bench$hi,
              "ETS(A,A,A): 1-day-ahead forecasts", "fc_ets_h1.png"))
```

One day ahead the ETS forecast sits on top of the actual demand for most of the year, inside a band of 1133.38 MW either side. The forecast reacts a day late at sharp turns. At the turn of the year it drops to about 20000 MW, below the actual demand, just as demand starts to recover from the year-end break.


```{r fc ets h7}
#| label: fc-ets-h7
print(plot_fc(bench$ets7, bench$ets7_lo, bench$ets7_hi,
              "ETS(A,A,A): 7-day-ahead forecasts", "fc_ets_h7.png"))
```

Seven days ahead the ETS forecast has no steady offset, but its band is very wide, 2799.08 MW either side of the forecast on average. That is why 98.4% of the actual values fall inside it. Because the forecast leans so heavily on the most recent week, it repeats unusual days a week later. It stays near 24000 MW in late December while the actual demand falls to 21335 MW on 25 December, and then it is too low in the first half of January, when it carries the year-end low forward. In the same way, the Easter dip, the dip around Freedom Day in late April and the spike in mid-August all show up in the forecast one week after they happen.


```{r fc arma h1 }
#| label: fc-arma-h1
print(plot_fc(bench$arma1, bench$arma1_lo, bench$arma1_hi,
              "Regression + AR(1): 1-day-ahead forecasts", "fc_arma_h1.png"))
```

One day ahead the regression with AR(1) errors also follows the actual demand closely, with a narrower band of 937.76 MW either side. The forecast is slightly above the actual demand on many days, which fits its mean error of −339.88 MW. It does not go deep enough in the Easter dip in early April, where it bottoms at about 23800 MW against an actual low of 22860 MW on 3 April. The year-end drop is in the right place, compared to the ETS because the year-end indicator is part of the regression.

```{r fc arma h7}
#| label: fc-arma-h7
print(plot_fc(bench$arma7, bench$arma7_lo, bench$arma7_hi,
              "Regression + AR(1): 7-day-ahead forecasts", "fc_arma_h7.png"))
```

Seven days ahead the regression forecast sits above the actual demand almost everywhere, mostly by 1000 to 2000 MW, because the AR(1) correction has mostly died out. The band is 1305.37 MW either side but moves up with the forecast, so the actual demand often falls below the lower edge, which gives the coverage of 66.6%. The gap is smallest in early June and largest at the start of January and around Easter and Freedom Day, where the forecast is about 3000 MW too high. The forecast still has the right weekly shape and gets the year-end drop right, so this plot shows the opposite problem to ETS. The regression knows the calendar but has the wrong level, while ETS follows the level but does not know the calendar.

## Discussion

Both approaches handle the weekly cycle the same way, with a fixed weekly pattern, and both leave the same weekly structure in their residuals, with spikes at lags 7, 14, 21 and 28. The difference is in the yearly cycle and the level of demand. The regression models the yearly cycle directly, with nine Fourier pairs and indicators for holidays, Easter and the year-end, and it gets the shape of the year right, including the year-end drop. But its level comes from a linear trend fixed on the training data, and when demand fell much faster in the test year the plain regression forecast 1122.71 MW too high on average. ETS(A,A,A) has no yearly term, so with alpha at 0.91 its level carries both the yearly cycle and the fall in demand. It does not know a holiday is coming and only reacts the day after, but it never drifts away from the actual level. So the regression captures the calendar better and ETS(A,A,A) follows the level better, and in this test year following the level mattered more. The same split decides the seven-day results, where ETS(A,A,A) is no better than the seasonal naive forecast, 1056.04 against 1058.72 MW, and the regression with AR(1) errors falls back towards the wrong level, 1236.37 MW.

One day ahead, both final models matched Eskom's own forecast. ETS(A,A,A) has an RMSE of 599.88 MW and an MAE of 442.86 MW against Eskom's 622.80 MW and 493.57 MW, and the regression with AR(1) errors has an RMSE of 606.36 MW and almost the same MAE as Eskom (493.03 MW). The plain regression only got there once the AR(1) errors were added, which add back about 70% of the previous day's gap between demand and the regression line. The RMSE differences from Eskom are small and I did not test whether they are statistically significant, so the fair conclusion is that both models are as good as Eskom's forecast one day ahead, with ETS(A,A,A) slightly ahead. I do not know how Eskom's forecast is produced. From the plots it seems to use the calendar, since it drops on holidays themselves, but it also has misses of its own, so I cannot say why it does not do better.

One day ahead the intervals of both models are close to reliable but a little too narrow, covering 92.60% of the test days for ETS(A,A,A) and 87.1% for the regression with AR(1) errors. For the regression the main cause is that the test errors are larger than the training errors the intervals are built from. For ETS(A,A,A) a few very large errors around holidays also play a part, since its residuals have heavier tails than the normal distribution the intervals assume. Seven days ahead neither set of intervals can be relied on. The ETS intervals cover 98.4% of the days because they are built for larger errors than the model makes, which makes them too wide to be useful, and the regression intervals cover only 66.6% because they are centred too high. ETS(A,A,A) has the lower CRPS at both horizons, 326.65 against 348.91 one day ahead and 602.15 against 799.94 seven days ahead.

There are a few limits to these results. I only have one test year, and it contains a much larger fall in demand than the earlier years (1696 MW between the 2025 and 2026 winters, against 450 MW to 680 MW before). In a year with a more normal fall the linear trend would be closer to the truth, so the gap between the two approaches may be smaller than it looks here. I did not test whether the differences from Eskom are statistically significant. I have no weather data, which means I cannot explain the high days such as 11 and 12 August 2026. My holiday list is built by hand and does not include bridge days or the low days in May 2024. All the intervals assume normal errors, while the ETS residuals have heavier tails. Finally, the parameters of every model were kept fixed for the whole test year. Refitting the regression during the year would let its trend catch up, but a straight line would still lag behind a sudden drop.

The results point to a model that has both strengths: the calendar terms of the regression together with a level that moves every day, like the ETS level. A state space model with a random-walk level and the same calendar regressors does this, and it is the starting point for Project 4, which uses the same data, the same test year and the same measures, so its results can be compared directly with the ones here.

```{r}
#| label: save-bench
saveRDS(bench, here::here("projects", "project-03-eskom-demand", "bench_p3.rds"))
```
